procedures.title: Procedures
procedures.description: Essential steps before, during, and after.

content.vitals_1: BP, HR, RR, temperature, pain, and SpO₂ should be assessed together, not in isolation.
content.vitals_2: Sudden changes or a worsening trend require reassessment and prompt communication to the team.
content.vitals_3: Document time, context, intervention taken, and patient response.
content.medications_1: Verify patient, med, dose, route, time, dilution, and documentation before administration.
content.medications_2: Allergies, interactions, and duplications need to be checked before med administration.
content.medications_3: If unsure about a dose or if a prescription is illegible, pause and confirm with the responsible team.
content.safety_1: Hand hygiene is the primary barrier against healthcare-associated infections.
content.safety_2: Patient identification must occur before meds, specimen collection, and procedures.
content.safety_3: Fall risk, pressure injury, and allergies should be visible in the plan of care.
content.procedures_1: Before the procedure: explain, confirm ID, gather supplies, and preserve privacy.
content.procedures_2: During: maintain proper technique, observe signs of discomfort, and communicate any complications.
content.procedures_3: After: discard materials, document findings, and monitor clinical response.

quickTips.tip_1: Use mind maps to review anatomy, pharmacology, and semiology.
quickTips.tip_2: Practice dose and drip rate calculations with short examples daily.
quickTips.tip_3: Turn protocols into checklists to memorize critical steps.
quickTips.tip_4: Review warning signs by system: respiratory, cardiovascular, neurological, and metabolic.

dailyTips.title: Daily Study Tip
items: Review a normal vital sign parameter and a warning sign before your next shift.
When studying medications, always associate class, indication, adverse effects, and nursing care.
Practice explaining a procedure in simple language, as if you were instructing a patient.
Create small safety checklists to translate theory into practical routine.
Set aside 10 minutes to review common abbreviations: BP, HR, RR, SpO₂, IM, IV, SC, and PO.
When studying a topic, ask: what do I observe, what do I document, and when do I communicate?
Review drip rate calculation with a simple example to maintain proficiency.
Study signs of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia by comparing symptoms and initial interventions.
Make flashcards of administration routes and commonly used sites in practice.
Review standard precautions: hands, PPE, disposal, and prevention of biological exposure.
Read a short protocol and condense the main steps into three bullet points.
Practice clinical reasoning: altered data + possible cause + first safe action.

vitals.intro: The foundation for assessing clinical stability and recognizing early deterioration.

sections.title: What to Observe
items: Blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature, pain, and SpO₂.
Compare current values with history, diagnosis, medications, and patient complaint.
Observe associated signs: diaphoresis, pallor, dyspnea, confusion, somnolence, or severe pain.

sections.title: Alert Points
items: A drop in SpO₂, altered mental status, hypotension, persistent tachycardia, or high fever require immediate attention.
A worsening trend may be more significant than an isolated value.
Reassess after intervention and document the clinical response.

sections.title: To Memorize
items: Always document time, patient position, O₂ device, and intervention taken.
Vital signs are objective data, but they must be interpreted within the clinical context.

medications.intro: Safety summary for medication administration and review.

sections.title: Before Administering
items: Confirm patient, med, dose, route, time, dilution, expiration, and prescription.
Check for allergies, interactions, duplications, and necessary parameters before the dose.
If the prescription is illegible or the dose is unusual, pause and confirm before administering.

sections.title: During and After
items: Observe for immediate reactions, pain, extravasation, nausea, dizziness, or allergic signs.
Document administration, time, route, site when applicable, and any complications.
High-risk meds require a double-check per institutional protocol.

sections.title: To Study
items: Review common classes: analgesics, antibiotics, anticoagulants, insulins, and anti-hypertensives.
Associate each class with key nursing care considerations.

safety.intro: Best practices to reduce risks and protect patient, student, and team.

sections.title: Priorities
items: Correct patient identification before any care, collection, medication, or procedure.
Perform hand hygiene at indicated times and use PPE appropriately.
Maintain a safe environment: call bell accessible, bed rails per risk, dry floor, and locked bed.

sections.title: Frequent Risks
items: Falls, pressure injuries, allergies, infection, medication errors, and communication failures.
Use objective shift report focusing on situation, background, assessment, and recommendation.
Report adverse events and near misses to improve processes.

sections.title: To Memorize
items: Safety begins before the technique: confirm, prepare, communicate, and document.
Simple checklists reduce oversight in repetitive routines.

procedures.intro: A quick framework for studying and performing procedures safely.

sections.title: Before
items: Read the prescription or indication, confirm ID, explain the procedure, and gather materials.
Assess for contraindications, allergies, pain, privacy, and need for assistance.
Organize the environment to prevent interruptions and contamination.

sections.title: During
items: Maintain clean or sterile technique as per procedure.
Observe for discomfort, bleeding, vital sign changes, or unexpected reactions.
Communicate complications and request support if there's a risk.

sections.title: After
items: Properly discard materials, perform hand hygiene, and ensure the patient is safe.
Document the procedure, findings, materials used, and patient's response.
Monitor for expected effects and signs of complications.
